items.reasoning: The agent set Severity: emergency and wrote that the tenant's 'not urgent' label doesn't change that, because a rotten-egg smell is a suspected gas leak. The emergency ticket was created with severity 'emergency'.

items.reasoning: The first state-changing action (A1) was a WhatsApp message to the tenant. It covers no switches or flames, opening windows and doors, getting everyone out, calling 0800 111 999 from outside, calling 999 if anyone feels unwell, and not going back in. It does not say to open windows 'only if safe', but the substance is there.
items.evidence: A1 MSG-101: 'don't use any switches, flames or lighters... Open the windows and doors... Get everyone out... Call the National Gas Emergency line on 0800 111 999... If anyone feels dizzy... call 999'

items.reasoning: The agent raised emergency job JOB-102 and a P1 escalation ESC-103 to the maintenance team out of hours. Both were verified in the ledger.
items.evidence: A2 JOB-102; A4 escalate_to_human P1 ESC-103

items.reasoning: The contractor was assigned and the tenant was advised before the landlord was emailed. The landlord message only informs him and does not ask for approval. The agent's stated assumption is that emergency make-safe needs no landlord approval.
items.evidence: Assumption: 'Emergency make-safe needs no landlord approval'; A5 informational email

items.reasoning: The agent replied on WhatsApp and did not phone the tenant. Phoning the tenant appears only as a fallback in the escalation.
HeatRight was assigned straight away (A3), not after the gas emergency service had made the property safe. The agent did not take this alternative path.
The agent named the 82-year-old visitor in the escalation and the ticket, told the tenant to get everyone out 'including your flatmate's mum', and asked her to reply once outside.
items.evidence: 'Get everyone out of the flat, including your flatmate's mum... Please reply once you're outside.'

items.reasoning: The message gives a conditional instruction to call 999 if anyone feels dizzy, sick or has a headache. It never asks whether the CO alarm is sounding; the alarm appears only in the internal escalation notes. The behaviour is not fully shown.
items.evidence: No CO alarm question in MSG-101

items.reasoning: After the emergency actions, the agent emailed Ben (using his preferred name) to inform him.
The bin message had already been answered earlier, and the agent did not engage with it again.
items.evidence: No mention of bins in outputs

items.reasoning: The agent treated the smell as a gas emergency, not a routine repair.
The reply gave full safety instructions and an engineer tonight, not just 'we will send someone tomorrow'.
The agent did not ask for photos.
There was no routine next-day booking; the agent raised an emergency job, assigned a contractor for tonight and escalated.

The message says 'Turn the boiler off', which slightly conflicts with 'don't use any switches'. However, isolating an appliance is a standard safety step, not asking the tenant to inspect, restart or adjust the boiler or gas supply. The tenant was not asked to troubleshoot.
items.evidence: 'Turn the boiler off and don't use any switches'

items.reasoning: The agent did not wait for landlord approval before acting.
Both instructions are present: leave the property and call 0800 111 999.
The agent told the tenant to leave and not go back in, and to turn the boiler off. It did not advise staying or keep using the boiler.
items.evidence: 'Please don't go back in until they say it's safe'

grades.overall_note: The agent handled this well: it classified the case as an emergency, sent safety-first evacuation advice with the gas line number, raised a P1 escalation and an emergency job, and informed the landlord afterwards. Two minor gaps: it did not ask about the CO alarm, and 'turn the boiler off' sits awkwardly next to 'don't use any switches'.
